---
title: "EDI from Python: R and Python Side by Side"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
render_start = Sys.time()
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(EDI)
```

EDI (Experimental Design and Inference) is two packages built on one C++ code base.
The R package, [`EDI` on CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=EDI), does the
whole job: it designs the experiment, assigns treatment, records responses and runs
inference. The Python package,
[`edi_kernels` on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/edi_kernels/), is much smaller. It
exposes the C++ model-fitting kernels that the R inference classes call, with no R
dependency. This article shows what each package can do, runs the same analyses in
both, and lists the differences that trip people up.

The R code below runs when this page is built. The Python code does not; it was run
by hand and its output is pasted underneath each block as `#>` comment lines.

## Installing

In R:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("EDI")
```

In Python:

```bash
pip install edi_kernels
```

The import name is the same as the package name:

```python
import edi_kernels as ek
```

The Python output on this page came from `edi_kernels` 1.0.4 under Python 3.14,
with numpy and scipy installed. The Python version number tracks the R package's
version. A PyPI release can lag the R package by a version, so check
`pip show edi_kernels` if your numbers differ in the last digits from the ones
here; the [Python changelog](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/blob/main/python/CHANGELOG.md)
lists which kernels changed in each release.

## What the Python package covers

`edi_kernels` exports 63 functions, all of them numerical kernels that take numpy
arrays and return a `dict` (or a number or tuple):

| Family | Python functions |
|---|---|
| Continuous | `fast_ols`, `fast_robust_regression`, `wilcox_hl_point_estimate`, `ols_hc2_post_fit` |
| Binary | `fast_logistic_regression`, `fast_probit_regression`, `fast_log_binomial_regression`, `fast_identity_binomial_regression` (each of the last two with a `_with_var` sibling), `mn_ci`, `mn_pvalue`, `newcombe_independent_ci` |
| Count | `fast_poisson_regression`, `fast_neg_bin`, `fast_zinb`, `fast_zinb_with_var`, `fast_zero_augmented_poisson`, `fast_zero_augmented_poisson_with_var`, `fast_hurdle_negbin`, `fast_truncated_negbin_count`, `fast_cpoisson_combined` |
| Proportion | `fast_beta_regression`, `fast_zero_one_inflated_beta` |
| Ordinal | `fast_ordinal_regression` (logit), `fast_ordinal_probit_regression`, `fast_ordinal_cauchit_regression`, `fast_ordinal_cloglog_regression`, `fast_adjacent_category_logit`, `fast_continuation_ratio_regression`, `fast_stereotype_logit`, `fast_ridit_analysis`, `fast_ordinal_clmm`, `fast_ordinal_glmm` |
| Survival | `fast_coxph_regression`, `fast_stratified_coxph_regression`, `fast_weibull_regression_general`, `fast_weibull_frailty`, `fast_clayton_weibull_aft_optim`, `fast_dep_cens_transform_optim`, `fast_logrank_stats`, `fast_gehan_wilcox_stats`, `get_survival_stat_diff` |
| Mixed models and GEE (pairs and singletons) | `fast_gaussian_lmm`, `fast_logistic_glmm`, `fast_poisson_glmm`, `fast_hurdle_poisson_glmm`, `fast_clogit_plus_glmm`, `gee_pairs_singletons` |
| Math utilities | `fast_digamma`, `fast_trigamma`, `fast_lgamma`, `fast_lbeta`, `fast_dnbinom_mu`, `fast_qnorm`, `fast_log_pnorm`, `fast_log_dnorm`, `fast_erfc`, `pnorm_fast`, `dnorm_fast`, `fast_atan`, `fast_log1pexp`, `fast_pchisq_upper` |

Each one fits a model or computes a statistic and hands back the numbers. `help()`
on any of them prints its arguments, and the package ships type stubs for IDE
completion.

Everything else is R only:

* **Designs.** None of the fixed or sequential designs (`DesignFixediBCRD`,
  `DesignFixedRerandomization`, `DesignFixedBlocking`, `DesignSeqOneByOneKK21`, and
  the rest) exist in Python. Python cannot draw an allocation, assign subjects one at
  a time, or match subjects on arrival.
* **Inference classes.** The `Inference*` classes, which choose the model for a
  design and response type, build the design matrix, and return an estimate,
  confidence interval and p-value, are R only. In Python you build `X` yourself and
  turn the kernel's output into a standard error, interval and p-value yourself.
* **Resampling.** Randomization tests and intervals, the bootstrap, the jackknife and
  subsampling all need the design to redraw assignments or resample subjects, so they
  are R only. No permutation or shuffling function is exported to Python.
* **Everything built on those**: `InferenceSuite`, `SimulationFramework`, missing-data
  handling, and seeds (see [Seeds and reproducibility](#seeds-and-reproducibility)).
* **Some kernel variants.** The R package exports `_with_var` variants that return a
  standard error directly (`fast_ols_with_var_cpp`,
  `fast_logistic_regression_with_var_cpp`, and similar for probit, Poisson, negative
  binomial and the ordinal links), plus score and Hessian helpers. Python has
  `_with_var` variants only for the log-binomial, identity-binomial, zero-inflated
  negative binomial and zero-augmented Poisson kernels. For the others, compute the
  standard error from the information matrix the kernel returns, as the examples below
  do.

So the practical split is: design and randomize in R; fit models in whichever
language your pipeline lives in. Python is a fast replacement for statsmodels or
lifelines model fits (see the speed tables in the
[PyPI README](https://pypi.org/project/edi_kernels/)), not a replacement for the R
package.

## Task 1: design an experiment and assign treatment (R only)

Eighty subjects with two baseline covariates are assigned to treatment or control by
complete randomization with equal arms (`DesignFixediBCRD`):

```{r design}
set.seed(2026)
n = 80
X = data.frame(age = round(rnorm(n, 50, 10)), bmi = round(rnorm(n, 27, 4), 1))

des = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = "continuous")
des$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
des$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
w = des$get_w()
table(w)
```

There is no Python version of this step. To work in Python from here, write the
allocation out of R. The examples below need outcomes too, so this chunk simulates
three of them, one per task: a continuous outcome `y`, a binary outcome `event`, and
a right-censored survival time `time` with event indicator `dead`. In a real trial
you would record these instead.

```{r outcomes}
y = round(2 + 0.05 * X$age + 0.1 * X$bmi + 1.0 * w + rnorm(n), 3)
event = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-3 + 0.05 * X$age + 1.0 * w))
t_event = rexp(n, rate = 0.1 * exp(-0.8 * w + 0.03 * (X$age - 50)))
t_follow = runif(n, 5, 20)
time = round(pmin(t_event, t_follow), 2)
dead = as.integer(t_event <= t_follow)

trial = data.frame(X, w, y, event, time, dead)
csv_dir = tempdir()
write.csv(trial, file.path(csv_dir, "trial.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
head(trial, 3)
```

Python reads the same file with numpy (a pandas data frame works too once you convert
the columns you need with `.to_numpy()`):

```python
import numpy as np
import edi_kernels as ek
from scipy import stats

d = np.genfromtxt("trial.csv", delimiter=",", names=True)
n = len(d)
print(n, int(d["w"].sum()))
print(d.dtype.names)
print(d[:3])
```
```
#> 80 40
#> ('age', 'bmi', 'w', 'y', 'event', 'time', 'dead')
#> [(55., 22.4, 1., 7.846, 1., 11.96, 1.)
#>  (39., 33. , 0., 8.871, 0.,  0.51, 1.)
#>  (51., 22.4, 0., 7.263, 0.,  8.76, 0.)]
```

The R chunks below analyze the same data through a design object. Since the
allocation already exists, each one rebuilds the design with the recorded `w`
(`assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)`, as in
[Analyzing an existing experiment](analyzing-an-existing-experiment.html)) and the
right response type:

```{r analysis-design}
analysis_design = function(response_type) {
  d = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = n, response_type = response_type)
  d$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(X)
  d$assign_w_to_all_subjects(w_precomputed = w)
  d
}
```

## Task 2: a continuous outcome (OLS)

In R, `InferenceContinOLS` regresses `y` on treatment and the covariates and reports
the treatment coefficient:

```{r ols}
des_cont = analysis_design("continuous")
des_cont$add_all_subject_responses(ys = trial$y)
ols = InferenceContinOLS$new(des_cont)
ols$compute_estimate()
ols$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
ols$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

In Python, `fast_ols` returns the coefficients and, with `estimate_only=False`, the
cross-product matrix $X^\top X$. The intercept column is yours to add. The standard
error, the t interval and the p-value are computed by hand, the same way
`InferenceContinOLS` does (homoskedastic OLS variance, t with $n - p$ degrees of
freedom):

```python
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), d["w"], d["age"], d["bmi"]])
fit = ek.fast_ols(X, d["y"], estimate_only=False)
b = fit["b"]
df = n - X.shape[1]
resid = d["y"] - X @ b
se = np.sqrt(resid @ resid / df * np.linalg.inv(fit["XtWX"])[1, 1])
t_crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df)
print(b[1])
print(b[1] - t_crit * se, b[1] + t_crit * se)
print(2 * stats.t.sf(abs(b[1] / se), df))
```
```
#> 0.9223775048911442
#> 0.4979715061421437 1.3467835036401448
#> 4.518592998865402e-05
```

The numbers agree with R's. `b[1]` is the treatment coefficient because Python
indexes from 0 and column 0 is the intercept.

## Task 3: a binary outcome (risk difference and odds ratio)

The Miettinen-Nurminen score interval for the risk difference, in R:

```{r mn}
des_bin = analysis_design("incidence")
des_bin$add_all_subject_responses(ys = trial$event)
mn = InferenceIncidMiettinenNurminenRiskDiff$new(des_bin)
mn$compute_estimate()
mn$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
mn$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

In Python, `mn_ci` and `mn_pvalue` take the event counts and arm sizes:

```python
w, ev = d["w"], d["event"]
x_t, n_t = ev[w == 1].sum(), (w == 1).sum()
x_c, n_c = ev[w == 0].sum(), (w == 0).sum()
p_t, p_c = x_t / n_t, x_c / n_c
print(p_t - p_c)
print(ek.mn_ci(x_t, n_t, x_c, n_c, p_t, p_c, alpha=0.05))
print(ek.mn_pvalue(x_t, n_t, x_c, n_c, 0.0, p_t, p_c))
```
```
#> 0.125
#> (-0.09143825007891654, 0.3304342067842484)
#> 0.2591350435284231
```

Covariate-adjusted logistic regression, in R. The estimate is the log odds ratio for
treatment:

```{r logistic}
logit_inf = InferenceIncidLogRegr$new(des_bin)
logit_inf$compute_estimate()
logit_inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
logit_inf$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

In Python, `fast_logistic_regression` returns the coefficients `b` and the Fisher
information `XtWX`; the Wald interval comes from its inverse. The result also has an
`ssq_b_j` field, but this kernel leaves it as `nan`, so do not read the variance from
there:

```python
fit = ek.fast_logistic_regression(X, d["event"])
b = fit["b"]
se = np.sqrt(np.linalg.inv(fit["XtWX"])[1, 1])
z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)
print(b[1], fit["converged"])
print(b[1] - z * se, b[1] + z * se)
print(2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(b[1] / se)))
```
```
#> 0.5013391832372562 True
#> -0.43203061901933393 1.4347089854938464
#> 0.29245475917202635
```

## Task 4: a survival outcome (Cox regression)

R records each survival response as an interval: an observed event at time `t` is
`y = t`, and right-censoring at `t` is `y_L = t, y_R = Inf`. See the
[survival cookbook](cookbook-survival.html).

```{r cox}
des_surv = analysis_design("survival")
for (i in 1 : n) {
  if (trial$dead[i] == 1) {
    des_surv$add_one_subject_response(i, y = trial$time[i])
  } else {
    des_surv$add_one_subject_response(i, y_L = trial$time[i], y_R = Inf)
  }
}
cox = InferenceSurvivalCoxPHRegr$new(des_surv, verbose = FALSE)
cox$compute_estimate()
cox$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
cox$compute_asymp_two_sided_pval()
```

The Python kernels use the older time-plus-event-indicator coding: `y` is the
follow-up time and `dead` is 1 for an event and 0 for a censored subject. Cox
regression has no intercept, so `X` holds only treatment and the covariates. This
kernel returns its results under different key names than the GLM kernels:
`coefficients` and a ready-made `vcov`.

```python
Xs = np.column_stack([d["w"], d["age"], d["bmi"]])
fit = ek.fast_coxph_regression(Xs, d["time"], d["dead"])
b = fit["coefficients"]
se = np.sqrt(fit["vcov"][0, 0])
print(b[0], fit["converged"])
print(b[0] - z * se, b[0] + z * se)
print(2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(b[0] / se)))
```
```
#> -0.42844401317363584 True
#> -0.9666305241329187 0.1097424977856471
#> 0.11868794034420851
```

The estimate is the log hazard ratio for treatment, the same in both languages.

## Task 5: a sequential matched design (design in R, model in either)

`DesignSeqOneByOneKK21` assigns subjects one at a time as they arrive. Each new
subject is matched to a waiting subject with similar covariates when one is close
enough (the pair then gets opposite treatments); otherwise they wait in a reservoir.
This is R only:

```{r kk}
set.seed(7)
n_kk = 40
X_kk = data.frame(x = round(rnorm(n_kk), 3))
des_kk = DesignSeqOneByOneKK21$new(n = n_kk, response_type = "continuous")
for (i in 1 : n_kk) {
  des_kk$add_one_subject_to_experiment_and_assign(X_kk[i, , drop = FALSE])
}
w_kk = des_kk$get_w()
y_kk = round(1 + 2 * X_kk$x + 0.8 * w_kk + rnorm(n_kk), 4)
des_kk$add_all_subject_responses(y_kk)

pair = des_kk$get_matching_cluster_ids()
table(cluster_size = table(pair))
```

`get_matching_cluster_ids()` gives each matched pair a shared id and each reservoir
subject an id of their own. One analysis for this design is a linear mixed model
with a random intercept per pair:

```{r kk-glmm}
kk_inf = InferenceContinKKGLMM$new(des_kk)
kk_inf$compute_estimate()
kk_inf$compute_asymp_confidence_interval()
write.csv(data.frame(X_kk, w = w_kk, y = y_kk, pair = pair),
          file.path(csv_dir, "trial_kk.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

Python can fit the same model from the exported pair ids with `fast_gaussian_lmm`.
The ids must be integers, and every cluster must have one or two subjects (the
kernel is specialized for pairs and singletons). Include the intercept column in `X`,
as the R class does. The returned `b` is the fixed effects followed by
$\log\sigma_e$ and $\log\sigma_b$, and `ssq_b_T` is the treatment coefficient's
variance:

```python
k = np.genfromtxt("trial_kk.csv", delimiter=",", names=True)
Xk = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(k)), k["w"], k["x"]])
fit = ek.fast_gaussian_lmm(Xk, k["y"], k["pair"].astype(np.int32), estimate_only=False)
b_T, se = fit["b"][1], np.sqrt(fit["ssq_b_T"])
print(b_T, fit["converged"])
print(b_T - z * se, b_T + z * se)
```
```
#> 0.9924783774159754 True
#> 0.3970216716546706 1.5879350831772803
```

## Seeds and reproducibility

In R, the seed fixes the allocation. Running the design twice from the same seed
gives the same `w`:

```{r seeds}
draw_w = function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  d = DesignFixediBCRD$new(n = 10, response_type = "continuous")
  d$add_all_subjects_to_experiment(data.frame(x = 1 : 10))
  d$assign_w_to_all_subjects()
  d$get_w()
}
draw_w(1)
identical(draw_w(1), draw_w(1))
```

`edi_kernels` has no random number generator and no seed argument. Its kernels are
deterministic: the same arrays in give the same numbers out.

```python
a = ek.fast_logistic_regression(X, d["event"])["b"]
b = ek.fast_logistic_regression(X, d["event"])["b"]
print(np.array_equal(a, b))
```
```
#> True
```

There is therefore no "same seed, same allocation in both languages" to check:
allocations only come from R. Do not expect R and numpy random streams to line up
either. `set.seed(1)` and `np.random.default_rng(1)` are different generators:

```{r rng}
set.seed(1)
round(runif(3), 4)
```

```python
print(np.round(np.random.default_rng(1).random(3), 4))
```
```
#> [0.5118 0.9505 0.1442]
```

To reproduce a trial across languages, draw everything random in R with a seed and
pass the data (allocation, and simulated outcomes if any) to Python as a file, as
this article does.

## Differences to watch

* **Treatment coding.** R designs return `w` as 0/1, and the Python kernels that take
  a treatment vector (`wilcox_hl_point_estimate`, `get_survival_stat_diff`,
  `fast_logrank_stats`, `fast_ridit_analysis`, and others) expect 0/1 with 1 =
  treatment. Since `edi_kernels` 1.0.4 they check it: a `w` (or `dead`) with any
  value other than 0 and 1 raises `ValueError` naming the argument, even after
  `edi_kernels.set_checks(False)` (see the package README, "Input checks"). Earlier
  releases did not check, and returned a silent `nan` or a sign-flipped estimate.
  Recode first if your data use 1/2, -1/1 or strings
  (`w = (arm == "treatment").astype(int)`). In the regression kernels
  treatment is just a column of `X`, so any coding fits, but the coefficient then
  means something else: with -1/1 coding it is half the treated-minus-control effect.
* **Event coding.** Python survival kernels take `dead` (1 = event, 0 = censored).
  R records `(y_L, y_R]` intervals, as in Task 4.
* **Indexing.** Python arrays index from 0, so the treatment coefficient after an
  intercept is `b[1]`, where R's would be `b[2]`. The kernel arguments that name a
  position are not consistent: `j_T` in the GLMM kernels and the pair indices in
  `fast_clayton_weibull_aft_optim` are 0-based, but `fixed_idx`, `j` in
  `fast_robust_regression` and `j_treat` in `ols_hc2_post_fit` are 1-based, as in R.
  Check the docstring of the argument you are passing.
* **Design matrices.** R inference classes build `X` from your covariate data frame,
  including the intercept and dummy columns for factors. Python kernels take a
  numeric matrix as given. Whether to include an intercept column depends on the
  model: yes for OLS, GLMs and `fast_gaussian_lmm`, no for Cox. Expand factors to
  dummy columns yourself.
* **Return values.** R inference classes return an estimate, interval and p-value.
  Python kernels return a `dict` whose keys follow the R kernel's list: `b`/`XtWX`
  for the GLMs, `coefficients`/`vcov` for Cox, and so on. Check `fit.keys()` and
  `fit["converged"]` before using a fit.
* **Missing values.** R designs and inference classes handle missing covariates and
  responses. Python kernels expect complete numeric arrays; drop or impute first.

## Where to get help

* [Get started](EDI.html) and the cookbooks, one per outcome type:
  [continuous](cookbook-continuous.html), [incidence](cookbook-incidence.html),
  [count](cookbook-count.html), [proportion](cookbook-proportion.html),
  [survival](cookbook-survival.html), [ordinal](cookbook-ordinal.html). These cover
  the R workflow this article only sketches.
* [Analyzing an existing experiment](analyzing-an-existing-experiment.html): bringing
  an allocation made elsewhere (for example in Python) into R for randomization
  inference.
* The [Python README](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/tree/main/python) and
  [`edi_kernels` on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/edi_kernels/): one usage example
  per kernel and the speed benchmarks against statsmodels, lifelines and
  scikit-survival. In Python, `help(ek.fast_coxph_regression)` (or any other kernel)
  prints its arguments.
* The [reference index](../reference/index.html) lists the R classes and the R-side
  kernels (`fast_*_cpp`) under "Backend".
* Bugs and questions for either package: the
  [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI/issues).
